Title: Reprinting Protected Resources, Archon Investigation, etc.

I think any reprint of an "in-demand", usable, hard-to-get old is a
great reprint! I believe this because Jyhad's value to me is as a game.
Cards that are hard to get and very useful - especially the ones that

new players entering the game and to having fun playing the game if you
can get them to start. I don't give a flying fornication how badly you
ream the trade value of my existing cards. I can still play with them -
*BUT* only if I have opponents!!!

To my mind, there is some argument in favor of *not* reprinting
Archon Investigation or Protected Resources - ever - on the basis
that they are overpowered cards that should never have been made
in the first place. (Their entire reason for existence is as
ultimate trumps - they punish an entire strategy all out of
proportion to its non-brokenness.)

That said, the cards are already out there, and in terms of
fairness the new players should probably have access to them
too. Unless VEKN were to see fit to ban them altogether for
being way stronger than they ought to be.

Josh

>To my mind, there is some argument in favor of *not* reprinting

>proportion to its non-brokenness.)

I like AI, actually. It's a good balance to the bleed decks; you can
jack that bleed up to 4 or better if you WANT to, but you're taking a
risk on it. Since a bleed for 3 is a pretty good slap-in-the-face for
most decks, it's still possible to make a quite effective deck that
bleeds for no more than 3 at a time. And you take a risk including AI
in your deck; since everyone knows about it, if someone refuses to
bleed you for more than 3 at a time, you have it sitting there as a
dead slot.

Protected Racehorses disturbs me a little bit more. To bleed through
it, you really DO need a weenie horde capable of bleeding for 2 with
each action; any deck relying on getting even just a bleed of 3 in
every so often will find itself in a world of hurt. However, I also
have to note that PR is, at the same time, not THAT good; a mixed
vote/bleed deck is often in a better situation than a pure-vote deck,
just because it's not necessarily screwed when someone drops Delaying
Tactics on a KRC... and if it sits next to an intercept predator, it
can actually get SOME damage through without worrying too much. PR
certainly doesn't belong in any deck except a vote deck; so I can't
see it being something to worry about ALL that much.

>That said, the cards are already out there, and in terms of
>fairness the new players should probably have access to them
>too. Unless VEKN were to see fit to ban them altogether for
>being way stronger than they ought to be.

And there is always this; they should get reprinted SOMEWHERE, if only
to make sure that newbies have a chance to grab hold.

-- Derek

Actually, truth be known, I can't ever manage to slip Protect Resources
in any deck, even the sort of voting decks that it allegedly does great
in. I can almost always find master cards that are better for the
deck in question in numbers too great to leave any room for the PR.
In my mind, Deflection is such a hoser for the kinds of bleed actions
which PR protects against that I'm challenged to understand its popularity.
The only reason I stick it with the big boys is because so many other
players claim it belongs there. Archon Investigation is sorta, kinda, the
same thing. Only the successful play of an AI is so much more devastating
than a simple deflection, that although I still think it's balanced - given
its cost - I question whether it might be too large an effect for a single
card being in the right place at the right time. (Kind of like my objection
to the design of Blood Moon in Magic - especially back when multilands were
convenient to use in so many decks.)

In any event, this kind of debate should be seen as being completely
orthogonal to reprint debates. If a card is broken, it should be banned
from the game. Then the question of reprinting it should be fairly moot.

The one concept I just HATEHATEHATEHATE is the idea certain people have
(and the DCI figures in quite prominently here!) is the idea that a
broken/thoroughly out-of-balance card should be allowed but NOT reprinted
using the logic that the problem is "lessened" if only a privileged few
can use a card but not the unwashed masses. BARF!

> That said, the cards are already out there, and in terms of
> fairness the new players should probably have access to them
> too. Unless VEKN were to see fit to ban them altogether for
> being way stronger than they ought to be.

Exactly. Why is that logic so difficult to comprehend for so many?

Fred

Getting your vamp burned isn't exactly balancing, is it? Maybe
I'm just biased, but I don't like *any* of the non-combat/diablerie
ways to burn vampires that got introduced post-Jyhad. (I'm not
sure how much I think Society of Leopold was a good idea either,
but Vulnerability is perfectly acceptable.) AI, Protect Thine
Own, Justicar Retribution, Sacrifice, Out of Control - all totally
wrong. (Banishment is wrong too, but it doesn't strictly "burn"
the vampire.) From my point of view, burning vampires was supposed
to be really hard, because they are your main avenue of accomplishing
things in the game, and as such, you were supposed to have to
work at combat to get it to happen, and if you burned via diablerie
you ran a substantial risk of getting your vampire burned as
well.

AI hurts bruise-bleed decks more than straight-bleed decks (or
so I've heard it argued), since a bruise-bleed may only be getting
one bleed action through in multiple turns and will want to make
it count with both an action card and a modifier (eg Govern +
Conditioning for 5-6). A straight bleed deck will probably be
bleeding on every action and may well be succeeding every time;
in those circumstances, having to stick to bleeds of 3 or less
isn't as much of a handicap.

> Protected Racehorses disturbs me a little bit more. To bleed through
> it, you really DO need a weenie horde capable of bleeding for 2 with
> each action; any deck relying on getting even just a bleed of 3 in
> every so often will find itself in a world of hurt. However, I also

> can actually get SOME damage through without worrying too much. PR
> certainly doesn't belong in any deck except a vote deck; so I can't
> see it being something to worry about ALL that much.

It could also go in any deck that uses the "oddball" tactics
to reduce their prey's pool, rather than bleeds - Smiling Jack,
Anarch Revolt, combat/Fame, etc. And yeah, it's not that amazingly
great most of the time, but it's a trump that (I think) shouldn't
really exist.)

Josh

Banishment is wrong because it can be called by Igo, the Hungry, who
can play a Bewitching Oration to banish Queen Anne. If he burns the
Edge, he can banish Democritus too.

Protect Thine Own is an eagle-eye hindsight screwup, because of its

burns IC members and Pulsed vampires, neither of which are inherently
abusive. And it also burns the poor bastard who's stacked up JS

therefore is going to fall by the wayside for the most part. Out of
Control is ridiculous; who knows why it was printed?

short time, with a very few cards. Nothing else can work so quickly,

Foreshadowing Destruction is awfully high-powered for a bleed card

with Scouting Missions; add FD when appropriate.

Yeah, but the plain old base damage vote is KRC. Free, and only does
3 points, and you have to send 1 elsewhere. Messy. Con Ag does more
at first, but ends up sucking worse for most of the time; Parity Shift
requires elaborate setup; Ancilla Empowerment and Domain Challenge are
dependent on your opponent. The plain old base bleed is 5: inferior
Govern + Condition. And it's possible to "up" it from there.

Voting also permits one's predator to block, which means that a vote
deck has to defeat two sets of defenses; all those BO's look great in
your hand until you need the extra stealth. :) It's more technically
difficult to get a vote passed than a bleed through, and you do less
damage overall with a vote. Advantage? The vote can land anywhere on
the table; the bleed must land on your prey.

out of Conditionings, and the rest combat so that any time someone
screws with you, you can knock their block off.

almost as well, although you do lose the "bleed for 1, think i have

saying that it is okay (or balanced) that a non-auspex or non-dominate
deck have zero defense against bleeds greater than 3? Because that is
what it sounds like. Being bled for more than three is really abusive
to be on the receiving end of. The only thing that keeps dominate decks
for bleeding for 7 every time (Govern + Command of the Beast +
Conditioning) is Archon Investigation. It is the only effective method
for a non-weenie rush deck to keep a stealth bleed deck under control as
a predator (if you dont' have auspex or dominate). I think a cost of 3
pool plus a card slot plus having to wait for the opportunity to play
Archon Investigation really does make the card balanced. If they are not
bleeding you for more than 3 then Archon Investigation just jams up your
hand, and if they look like they could bleed you for more than three
then most players will hold on to it just in case. This takes up a
valuable card slot. The card slot is the most expensive price of the
card. Having to hold onto one effectively reduces your hand size which

Bleed does not NEED to be weak against combat, bloat, OR intercept,
however; the trick lies in the deck construction. A Ventrue/!Ventrue
DOM/FOR bleed deck is not vulnerable to combat. A weenie Dominate
horde will overrun Minion Tap/5th. Malk S&B will beat intercept.

even that can be somewhat negated; interestingly enough, by the same
strategy that hoses AI (more bleeds for less).

against combat, bloat, and intercept, by diluting the focus of their
bleeds over multiple actions; and this moves the bleed defense away
from bleed bounce (the universally reliable one) and more towards the
center. AI is not a functional defense by itself. But its
supplemental action helps other defenses become viable. Would I have
created it? ...No. If I were on the review team, would I permit it
by without complaint? ...No. Do I want to see it banned since it got
here anyway? ...No.

Conditioning is strong, but the difference between "1 blood" and
"free" is enormous in V:TES, much more so than the difference between
"1 blood" and "2 blood". "free" means "anytime, forever", and that
can be VERY important since a deck relying on Scouting Mission/FD will
be bleeding for either 3 or 5 *totally* for free; and it can use the
blood it's not spending for Governs or Conditions as Blood Doll
fodder.

The other reason is that FD's condition is applicable much more often
than people realize; most decks will transfer out approximately 14-16
pool of vampires to start with, and so will be operating from the word
"go" at around 15 pool. It only takes a couple quick bleeds or votes
to reduce someone to 9, and then FD's advantage begins to really kick
in. And you can always cycle it for an extra +1 bleed if you need to
move one out of your hand, helping you get to the range where its
superior is useful. Later in the game it becomes even MORE useful,
when vampires are low on blood and EVERYONE's pool is within FD's
range; a free bleed for 1 that suddenly becomes 4 and the vampire
doesn't need to hunt next turn, or a 1-blood bleed for 3 that suddenly
becomes 6... these get very nasty.

defense; the weenie horde can bleed for 15 or 20.
Likewise, AI hurts the Arika deck more; you lose your whole deck, and
the weenie deck can afford to lose a minion a turn, even.
The problem is that the nature of Dominate bleed available to small guys
punishes you for playing big vamps; you can't block all the actions, rush
all the guys, etc. of the weenies, but you can stuff a single big bleed a
turn without having to have an "anti-deck."
The problem is Samson. The problem is Ohanna. The problem is Mustafa.
The problem is Royce. The problem is Christine Boscacci.
But, most of all, the problem WAS Misdirection. Which has been fixed,
and we'll have to see just how well weenie dominate bleed (or tap-and-bleed)

for half their blood, they'll slow down a lot.

The "problem" with AI, somewhat, is that it has no "cheeze detector."
It's a great anti-cheeze card, but it also hoses you for playing big vamps
that bleed. You have less actions, you NEED to bleed for more than 3 at
time to oust someone competitively. But, AI makes Arika just as dead as
Ozmo.

But, (to get back to disagreeing, and tie in) not being able to bleed
for more than 3 with all 4 of your Malkavians really isn't hurting you too
much, and gives your prey a fighting chance.

You are kidding me, right?

you want to block them? Oh, wait. Nothing. And 1 and 2 cap vampires with

that it is okay (or balanced) that a non-auspex or non-dominate deck have zero
defense against bleeds greater than 3?>>

They have plenty of defenses--they just need to use them. Animalism allows for
very effective intercept. Rush combat. Vote the bleeder across the table. Gain
infinite pool. Saying the AI is the only possible defense against large bleed
decks is just silly.

>>Because that is what it sounds like. Being bled for more than three is
really abusive to be on the receiving end of. The only thing that keeps
dominate decks for bleeding for 7 every time (Govern + Command of the Beast +
Conditioning) is Archon Investigation. >>

Well, that and that if they do get bounced (yes, Iam aware that only Dominate
or Auspex can bounce something), they are bleeding their grand prey for 7. And
bleed decks that can consistiently bleed for 7 on every action won't have a
stick of combat defense, and will be killed by combat decks quite nicely.

Large bleeds have existed since day one of the game. The game existed quite
nicely before AI was invented. If they wanted to create extra bleed defense,
fine--Elder Intervention is a perfectly balanced, solid card specifically for
bleed defense. AI, which costs negative pool and burns a vampire? Not so much.

>>Zebulon plays obedience,>>

If Zebulon has enough Obediance and Wake (he is tapped out from bleeding you
for 7, remember?) to reliably stop a Rush deck, he isn't going to be bleeding
for 7 on a regular basis. Or have much stealth to deal with the intercept deck
he might very well be sitting next to.

the Bum's Rush, denying Lupo the Manuver? Or because it wasn't someone using a
Press?

>>A little combat defense goes a long way in a stealth bleed deck.>>

A *little* combat defense in a S+B deck gets you nowhere--it is unreliable and
hard to match up the cards you need. A lot of combat defense in a S+B deck is
helpful, but it keeps you from bleeding people for 7 on a regular basis. The
deck simply can't do it all at once.

>>So Sorry, Lupo. You get to fail at your rush action to send Zebulon to
torpor.>>

Uhh, yeah. That is going to work. S+B decks that have reliable combat defense
aren't the quick and deadly bleeders that you seem to think warrant the
existance of AI. They don't bleed for as much and for as often, making them
much slower and much more manageable--it is likely that such a S+B deck could
bleed you reliably for about 3 an action, but 7? I think not.

In article <a9bb3tonn8r3knkuv...@4ax.com>,

Derek Ray <lor...@yahoo.com> wrote:
> On Mon, 11 Dec 2000 22:12:18 -0600, James Hamblin
> <ham...@math.wisc.edu> wrote:
>
> >
> >
> >I don't see FD as significantly more powerful than Conditioning. The
> >cost of a blood seems to offset the disadvantage of not being always
> >able to play superior FD. Unless you think Conditioning is "awfully
> >high-powered"?
>
> Conditioning is strong, but the difference between "1 blood" and
> "free" is enormous in V:TES, much more so than the difference between
> "1 blood" and "2 blood". "free" means "anytime, forever", and that
> can be VERY important since a deck relying on Scouting Mission/FD will
> be bleeding for either 3 or 5 *totally* for free; and it can use the
> blood it's not spending for Governs or Conditions as Blood Doll
> fodder.

I think this is an interesting point. Conditioning probably
*is* quite high-powered, mainly because it costs 1 blood but
inflicts 2/3 pool of damage on your prey (or whoever the lucky
recipient is). In general 1 blood is roughly equivalent (if
slightly inferior) to 1 pool, so turning 1 blood into 3 damage
is a pretty good trade.

Of course, a vote deck can turn 0 blood into 3 damage with a
KRC, and a combat deck can turn 0 blood into 10 damage with
a Rush, Signpost, Undead Strength, Sideslip, Nimble Feet,
Undead Strength (Grapple if necessary). Those can require more
cards to implement, though.

Still, the principle seems to be that it's easier to inflict
pool damage than to gain pool. You can gain 1 for a card and
a master phase action with Ascendance, or turn a bunch of vamp
blood into pool with a Minion Tap, or gain an ongoing source of
pool with an Eco Terrorists (for a 2 pool investment) or Powerbase
Chicago (1 pool), or 2 for an action and a card with Art Scam.

I wonder if the crux of this argument isn't just that bleeding is
able to do the most damage in the least time (eg you can get a
bleed of six for two cards and two blood, or eight w/an Inner
Circle vamp). In the most winning-is-everything oriented games,
then, people will only play the most effective decks, which will
probably be either strong bleed decks, fast combat decks (weenie
combat, as some here have been calling it - though in my experience
I have never seen a truly non-weenie combat deck that had a good
chance of winning games, let alone tournaments), and (probably
presence-based) fast vote decks. Possibly some 5th/Tap bloat as
well, generally backing up either bleed or vote; those ToGP/Parity
Shift/etc decks might show up too. But it seems to me that perhaps
people object to seeing this kind of thing all the time, get bored
with it, and want the clans and decktypes that aren't the most
competitive to show up/be playable in tournaments, and therefore
like having Archon Investigation available to make the bleed decks
a little slower and less efficient (or more dead, if they do get
caught by an AI).

I'm don't really think AI is the right way to accomplish that. I'd
be happier either seeing the other clans/skills get cards that let
them compete on the same level, or else reducing the power of
the "dominant" (not necessarily "dominate", ha ha) types. I know
that if that meant serious errata or bannings, a lot of people would
be pretty pissed off about that too, but I dunno, it might be better
than having so many non-competitive cards out there.

Maybe it's just that I want to have my cake and eat it too - I like
competitive games, and I like tournaments. I know some people are
happy enough playing their non-competitive decks against each other
in friendly games (which may even be specified as being for "fun"
or "silly" or "experimental" decks), but I'd like to see them be
playable in tournaments, if the concept is reasonable in the first
place.

> The other reason is that FD's condition is applicable much more often
> than people realize; most decks will transfer out approximately 14-16
> pool of vampires to start with, and so will be operating from the word
> "go" at around 15 pool. It only takes a couple quick bleeds or votes
> to reduce someone to 9, and then FD's advantage begins to really kick
> in. And you can always cycle it for an extra +1 bleed if you need to
> move one out of your hand, helping you get to the range where its
> superior is useful. Later in the game it becomes even MORE useful,
> when vampires are low on blood and EVERYONE's pool is within FD's
> range; a free bleed for 1 that suddenly becomes 4 and the vampire
> doesn't need to hunt next turn, or a 1-blood bleed for 3 that suddenly
> becomes 6... these get very nasty.

Oh, I'm well aware that Foreshadowing Destruction's superior is
very often playable. I'm just saying that going over 3 bleed is
awfully easy to do, and burning a vamp for doing it is a very harsh
punishment. The situation is identical for superior Conditioning,
or for a Bonding with a Pulsed or IC vampire, or a Govern with a
+1 bleed vampire.

Josh

Let's face it: there are a bunch of clans and skills that are
*not* tournament-competitive, even *with* Archon Investigation.
The solution isn't to put in more Methuselah-based strategy
hosers, it's to give them cards that will make them playable.

> But it is okay if on turn two you get bled by Christina
Bocasci,Ohanna,
> and Royce, for 18. This is possible if your predatore plays either a
> Dreams of the Sphinx or a Info Highway on the first round and a
dominate
> skill card on the second round. All you have to do is to go first in
a
> four player game and have this thing bleeding you. If you want to get
> out a six cap or higher you get to take a bleed for 18. Thanks for
> playing.

Are you happier if you get bled on turn two by Christine, Ohanna,
and Samson for 9, and then for another 9 on turn 3? If you have
out no more than one vampire, you will be just as vulnerable to
new-Misdirection as old-Misdirection. (math note - your pred has
to get out 3 2-caps, not Royce, to be able to play two 1-cost
cards with each, and can only put DOM on one of them, getting to
16 bleed, not 18.)

Weenie decks are inherently efficient at doing lots of pool
damage very quickly; they are also inherently vulnerable to
being sent to torpor with no more than three points of damage
per vampire, and to being blocked by someone with lots of untaps.
Archon Investigation can't solve this all by itself; it's a basic
feature of the game that more actions is better and that your
minion cards mostly don't care what capacity your vampires are.
It's perhaps an unfortunate feature, but to seriously alter it
would require serious changes to the rules or the universe of
available cards.

> > Bounce is not the only, or always the best way to deal with bleed,
but
> > every clan has at least some way to deal with a bleed deck. If they
> > didn't more tourney winning decks would include AI and PR, because
> > bleed is sure as heck going to show up.
>
> So your conclusiton to your arguement is that AI and PR are not

tournament
> winning deck? That is quite a reversal of position. Perhaps you
should
> argue that bleed bounce is broken because it effectively hoses a core
> strategy.

If AI was really the only thing holding mega-bleeds down, shouldn't
it show up in more tourney-winning decks? I hesitate to do another
detailed analysis of The Lasombra's tourney-winning-decks archive
(because it's so thorough! cringe!), but on a quick search through,
I find thirteen decks out of seventy-three (~18%) that had Archon
Investigation in them. Of those thirteen, nine also had at least
5 bleed-bounce cards in them. Of the thirteen, four had more than
one AI, and all of those also had Deflections.

I should also look at how many of the 73 tourney-winners had
Dominate or Auspex and bounce in them, but that would take too
long for right now. ;-) Suffice to say that it looks to me
like, although AI's effect is certainly extreme, and it doubtless
has a "fear effect" keeping tourney players from bleeding for
more than 3 too often (unless with weenies they don't mind losing -
which is the opposite of the desired effect, isn't it?). But
since not that many winners are actually *playing* with it, it
must not be the only way to win tournaments - ie not *necessary*
to keep the bleeders from always killing you.

Josh

Seems unlikely. We don't seem to have statistics available for

If you're playing non-weenie rush, then you should presumably have some
other method of defense (multiple Blood Dolls, Minion Tap, untap &
intercept, something...) or you're just asking for trouble. If you're
playing Weenie Rush and run into a lot of Obedience, the Haven
Uncovereds will help out...throw in a couple more the next time around.

[intercept as a defense]

> Totally made inefficent (with the exception of the clans who have
> access to Auspex and therefore bleed bounce) by cards such as Elder
> Impersonation, Day Operation, Horrific Countenance, and Blanket of
> Night.

And Seduction, as mentioned elsewhere; and let's not forget Daring the
Dawn...

Putting all your eggs in one basket (loading up one minion with all of
your permanent intercept) is never a good idea. Avoiding this saves
you from Elder Impersonation, Blanket of Night, and Seduction. Day
Operation, Daring the Dawn, and Horrific Countenance are meant to be
big. That's why their cost (though I admit Freak Drive or MotSB/Rapid
Healing are a pretty no-brainer combo) is rather high. Still, this
extends the combo by two more cards, bringing it up to, what...GtU,
Conditioning, unblockable action mod, Freak/MotSB, Rapid Healing...a 5
card combo (6 with Command of the Beast) that causes 6 or 7 pool loss.
Pretty much the same as a Bum's Rush, TS, IG, Undead Strength,
(Disarm), Decapitate. If you have no bleed defense, then you're in
trouble. If you have no combat defense, you're in trouble. I don't
see the difference.

It appears that your problem is more with unblockable actions rather
than with large bleeds...

> Bloat decks have bleed defense: gain more pool than the
> > bleed deck is taking away.
>
> I have never, ever seen a bloat deck who could keep up with being bled
> for 6 with each bleed.

It can be done. This weekend, I outlasted a standard Malk S&B deck
that was hammering me with Ozmo and Didi Meyers. Minion Tap, 5th,
Parity Shift, ToGP'ed my predator once to bring him down 8 pool, and
every once in a while, I tested his stealth with 2nd Tradition, my only
intercept in the deck. It worked once, and I destroyed Ozmo.
Unfortunately, I didn't have a Decapitate in hand, but I did get the
Disarm off. Ozmo never bothered me again.

My ToGP deck has about 6 2nd Traditions, and that's the only intercept
in the deck, yet I was able to stop the S&B by letting him jam on
stealth, discard a lot of it, and then 2nd Tradition a couple of times,
along with the Minion Tap/Parity Shift pool gain. This in a deck that
had no bounce, no AI, and only second-rate at best (according to you)
options available to it. Did I mention that I was playing Nosferatu?
And I only had Sheldon and Chester out?

> > There were already plenty of ways to deal with bleed decks. More
> > wouldn't have been necessarily bad. But AI has negative cost, and
> > BURNS a vampire.
>
> Burning a vampire is exactly what makes power bleeders fear it. Once
> again, AI's power isn't in the fact that it burns one vampire, but

No, AI's power *is* in the fact that it burns a vampire. The fear of
this is secondary. AI is approximately as powerful as ToGP...same pool
cost, but doesn't require a Justicar; requires a bleed of > 3, instead;
it burns the vampire as opposed to taking control of it; the vampire is
gone, there is no possibility of another Methuselah usurping control of
it by outbidding or another ToGP/Corruption. For a cost of 3 pool, you
have cancelled a bleed of at least 4, and you have effectively bled the
acting Methuselah for the influence cost of the vampire; perhaps this
is as little as 1, probably more like 4 or 5.

> > > Because that is
> > > what it sounds like. Being bled for more than three is really
> abusive
> > > to be on the receiving end of.
> >
> > I really don't know about "abusive".
>
> "Abusive" is when you feel you have been abused. Simply that.

No, that's "victimized". "Abusive" refers to the combination itself,
or to the person dishing out the abuse. And being bled for more than 3
hurts, but it's just the same as losing a vampire of equal capacity due
to combat, Banishment, ToGP, Corruption, etc.

> And you are arguing that a defense against bleeding for clans without
> auspex or dominate needs to be removed from the game. Maybe, you
> should try to play a deck without those two disciplines and no AI's,
> and see how you hold up against a Malk stealth-bleed.

As mentioned, it works.

> Please explain to me how eliminating AI helps those clans without
> dominate or auspex against power bleeds.

It does not help nor hurt them, in the long run. What it does is hurt
a valid deck archetype, namely, bleed. Decks that are going to bleed
are not going to stop or slow down just because they think an AI is
going to pop up. At worst, they figure that someone will pull one AI
during the course of the game, and they'll lose a minion, which hurts,
but isn't going to make them change their basic strategy.

[snip flamage]

> Removing defenses against stealth-bleed only makes that strategy more
> effective. Especially more effective against clans without

AI is, at best, a strong defense that is unreliable. Deflection is a
weaker (in terms of resource destruction), more reliable defense.

> bleed-bounce. Even weenie rush has a problem with dominate because of
> obedience and rabble razing.

Well, I don't see what dominate has to do with Rabble Razing, but yes,
Obedience shuts down a lot of rush. However, there are ways around
that...Haven Uncovered works really well, as would Contract, and
playing Obedience rules out weenie bleed, doesn't it? A lot of rush
decks step up to the 5 or 6 capacity range (or Beast-range), and most
efficient S&B decks stay around 5 capacity (Didi, Ozmo, Zebulon),
ruling out Obedience once again.

> Actually what this statement says is that I have played many effective
> rush decks using many different sized vampire. I have experience what
> it is like to have a stealth bleed deck beside me that actually has
> combat defense built into it. Often this combat defence occurs in the
> form of 8 dodges and 8 fake outs. This is often enough to make a rush

8 dodges and 8 fake outs is pretty weak combat defense, if you ask me.
I suppose it depends on what sort of combat you're playing, but if you
can't get about 2 maneuvers per combat, and can't beat dodge (much less
S:CE), you're not doing something right. 8 maneuvers and 8 dodges
isn't enough to get more than 1 or 2 of each per combat, and at 2,
you're going to run out really quickly.

> deck not torporize a minion on every rush action. A rush deck that
> fails to do that will stall. A rush deck that stalls is a rush deck
> that fails.

No, a rush deck doesn't necessarily stall with one failed rush action.
Sure, if you can torporize on every single action, you're doing good,
but the game isn't going to go straight to hell just because you failed
one rush. Sometimes it will, but not always, perhaps not even often.
Yeah, 4 or 5 or 6 failed rushes will definitely add up, though.

> A rush deck can mutilate a stealth bleed predator, but in doing so
> gives both his prey and his grand predator a free ride. This only
> compounds the problems a rush deck faces. As his grand-predator
> becomes his predator, the rush deck faces a even tougher challenge,
> holding off a more powerful predator than his previous one.

Depends on the table size. At a 4-player table, if his prey is having
an easy time, the grand-predator should not be, so it all evens out.
Maybe he'll acquire a new, weak predator, and then he can work on his
prey again, and get back to equilibrium. At a 5-player table, yeah,
that happens, but those are the risks you take. Tough.

I would also submit that Protracted Racehorses, I mean Protected
Resources would be more balanced as a Unique Location (as mentioned
elsewhere), or if it had a burn clause (less preferred), and might not
be out of flavor in Final Nights, as some of those clans are more
secluded and more able to insulate themselves from the Jyhad, perhaps.
The problem with it as written is that there is no way to remove it or
get around it, and there are no requirements (aside from the "can't
bleed" clause, which isn't that hard for a deck that doesn't focus on
bleeding) for playing it, which is out of character for Jyhad/V:tES in
general.

Xian

Messages.Author: Joshua Duffin
Messages.Body:
In article <B65BCA66.14AE%sp...@socrates.gatech.edu>,

Pat Ricochet <sp...@socrates.gatech.edu> wrote:
> > And if you argue that Archon Investigation costs 3 pool because
> > that's the number printed in the lower left, you could also
> > say that Minion Tap costs 0 pool and doesn't give you any. It
> > only gains you pool if you actually choose to take some off your
> > minion...

> You could say that, and in some cases, people play it to gain
zero pool,
> just to cycle the card. But, you're still moving onto *effects*.
> Archon Investigation *does* cost 3 Pool.
> Minion Tap *does* cost 0 Pool.

Effects are inseparable from costs. If the card isn't Reversed,
you get the effect along with the cost, and if it *is* Reversed,
you don't pay the cost.

> This whole blathering about "negative cost" to make AI look
broken or
> too powerful is pure number shuffling and doublespeak. "Cost" has a
defined
> meaning in V:tES, and saying that "AI costs 3 pool" is simply the
truth, and
> doesn't imply that the person making the statement has lost all the
> subtleties of the card and the game. As I said before,
this "negative cost"
> math implies that Deflection costs negative pool every time it's
> played...but there are other issues, of course.

Yeah, and that's what makes Deflection so much better than
*blocking* a bleed, isn't it?

> Please stick to clearly addressing those issues when making your
points
> instead of persisting in including this ridiculous "negative pool"
> metric/argument.

What's different about Archon Investigation - and what makes
it worth mentioning the "cost" issue - is that its printed
cost is only indirectly related to its actual cost. If you
can play AI at all, you were losing more than three pool to a
bleed. That "3" in the lower left corner isn't a "normal" cost,
because the effect of the card will save you at least four pool.
And if it's Sudden Reversed, you don't pay the 3 pool either.
So: all that "3" does is define the minimum "swing" you gain by
playing the card: at least 1 pool. If it were a 4, you would gain
at least 0 pool by playing it; if it were a 2, you would gain at
least 2 pool by playing it. As such, taking the effect of the
card when played into consideration along with the printed "3"
is just as reasonable and accurate as taking the effect of
Ascendance (gain 1 pool) into consideration when discussing the
costs and benefits of that card.

Saying that AI costs 3 pool, while technically accurate, *does*
ignore its effects, because if you can't pay the cost, you can't
take the bleed either.

Josh

> vampire in combat with one of your minions if that vampire is dealing
> more than 3 damage with a strike." Maybe someday we will need it if
> Potence combat ever gets out of control.

If you think so, we may simply disagree on the appropriateness
of hoser cards. To my mind, that card would never be necessary
as long as nobody's introducing broken Potence cards into the
game (like Elastic Iron-Hot Arms of Death or something, for those
who remember that).

For me, hosers are simply not an appropriate method of (trying
to) balance VTES. Clan hosers suck too, but strategy hosers
are even worse. The game should be about finding balances and
countermeasure *within* the structure of vampire interaction,
not by coming up with huge-effect master cards to counter any
conceivable difficulty.

If the bleed cards are not broken in and of themselves, then
a card like Archon Investigation should not be necessary to
deal with them. If they *are* broken, they are what should be
banned or fixed. To me, printing "magic bullet" cards is the
lamest possible attempt at a solution; it's what games like
Star Wars (great quotes, not much of a game) and Magic (fun if
you don't mind spending the money and time) do. VTES has a far
more elegant and balanced system than they do, and it should
use that and try to keep it.

Josh

>> Why it was created isn't what I'm discussing; it's here now, and we're
>> stuck with it unless we ban it. The question is, it is so unbalancing
>> that it needs to be banned? Or would banning it tip the scale too far
>> towards the bleed decks?
>
>Seems unlikely. We don't seem to have statistics available for
>this (since, sadly, The Lasombra only started collecting tourney-
>winning decks in 1997, and DejaNews doesn't go back even that
>far now...), but did bleed decks win all the time, and necessitate
>bounce in every tourney deck, before the VTES printing in 1995?
>I doubt it (though I don't know enough about the tourney scene
>of that time to say for sure).

Neither do I. But I note that Archon Investigation, Protected
Resources, and Elder Intervention were created specifically in the
V:TES printing, and such powerful cards being added in what was
nominally a reprint of the base set indicate that bleed decks were, in
fact, that powerful, and that stealth bleed was THE premier deck of
the time.

Many cards have been added since then, so the equation becomes a lot
more fuzzy and requires re-looking at.

>> Bleed does not NEED to be weak against combat, bloat, OR intercept,
>> however; the trick lies in the deck construction. A Ventrue/!Ventrue
>> DOM/FOR bleed deck is not vulnerable to combat. A weenie Dominate
>> horde will overrun Minion Tap/5th. Malk S&B will beat intercept.
>> Bleed bounce is the strongest natural counter to a bleed deck, and
>> even that can be somewhat negated; interestingly enough, by the same
>> strategy that hoses AI (more bleeds for less).
>
>But a DOM/FOR bleed deck *is* vulnerable to intercept (at least
>the blocking part); a weenie dom horde is vulnerable to combat;
>Malk S&B is vulnerable to combat, bounce, and probably bloat.
>You don't have to be weak against *all* these defenses, but if
>you're not weak against *any* of them you're probably not bleeding
>for much either.

Certainly. But the point was that ALL bleed decks are vulnerable to
bounce, and the other three defense strategies all have a visible weak
point. AI's existence helps shore up that weak point, if you don't
wish to include bounce.

As it stands right now, you KNOW there will be bleed decks at any
given tournament. You can be pretty sure that at least a couple of
them will be going for more-than-3 at any given moment, and will have
a way to get it past the plain old zero-stealth block. So you can
include bounce, and not worry about what type of deck shows up. Or
you can take a risk, and go with combat, bloat, or intercept. Each is
vulnerable to a very common type of strategy; AI helps each of these
defenses to some degree by providing a "fear" deterrent. Without that
deterrent's EXISTENCE, it is very dangerous to play any type of deck
that doesn't include bounce; a bad roll on seating position will nail
you. If you intend to attempt to win, it would be silly to even
CONSIDER decks without bounce. It doesn't matter if your intercept
deck contains an AI or not (although it probably should; those Day Ops
really suck), just the fact that a bleed deck has to WORRY matters.

Bleed decks are hardly hamstrung by AI. If you want to bleed for more
than 3, fine. I've made multiple decks that do just that. But you
know what? If you're moving along and dropping multiple big bleeds
and get a minion burned, yeah it slows you down, but it's probably not
going to stop you cold unless you're doing the "Etrius bleeds for 10!"
stunt or something. I know that if I build a bleed deck, I will
deliberately ignore one of the defense types; usually I'll include
combat defense and plenty of bleed oomph, and go a little lighter on
the stealth, as most people are well aware of the "don't block them"
theory regarding stealth/bleed. I hate getting caught behind a Minion
Tap for 10, and getting my minions beat up is never a good thing. And
I also ignore the threat of Archon Investigation. Sure, someone will
drop it on me eventually. I just try not to make any given minion
that much 'better' than any other. It happened in my Tzimisce
Pulse/Changeling deck; I had 3 Pulsed guys out and made the mistake of
using Changeling to "oomph" a bleed instead of saving it for stealth,
and poof. The deck still got 3 VP that game.

-- Derek
Jack-Booted Thug of Atlanta

>> Frankly, AI does not hose a core strategy. It doesn't burn you if

>> greater than 3. What it does do is make you compensate for it, and

No, it makes you fear *bumping* the bleed of your Inner Circle Member.
If that's your focus, you should spend your efforts railing against Justicar
Retribution, which burns ALL IC and Pulsed bleeders, whether or not they
even attempt to remove pool.
But, I don't see exactly Justicar Retribution hitting tables left and
right at tournaments.

> That fear shouldn't be present. I should worry if i'll be bounced, or
> blocked, or beat up next turn, because that is fear i can plan for, but
> short of malks bleeding out of turn and SRing the AI, there is no way
> for me to deal with it. That, IMHO, is what makes it bad for the game.

People still play, and win, with big bleed decks. But, it's not the
only deck kind that is played, or wins. This, IMHO, sounds like a good
arrangement. Big bleed is a viable, powerful, but counterable strategy.

Lemme try and bring out the basic disagreement, here.

If AI was so broken, no one would ever play or win with big bleed. Is
there some "total lack of big bleed" or "no one can win with big bleed"
mechanic in your (all of you, that is, railing against AI) local playgroup?
I just don't see an existing problem to be fixed, just another
possibility of the metagame. If you fear AI, don't play big bleed, and
people will stop playing AI so much. If you fear intercept so much, play
decks that only take 0-stealth actions. The evidence pulled up that AI *is*
played in tournament winning decks means that skilled players think it's
worthwhile. The fact that a majority did NOT have AI seems, to me, to imply
that the card isn't all powerful, it's just another option that has settled
into about as much use as any other card or strategy.

If you DO see a problem in the game as it is played often (say, as DI is
beginning to see a LOT of play and get grumbled at), or that *no* one plays
big bleed decks, then be clear. But, it's hard to call a card that's been
around so long "broken" or "bad for the game" when the game seems to toodle
along just fine with it's existence, with the card nor it's intended
victim-strategy seeing too much or too little play.

Also, for PR, AI, and Justicar Retribution, do the critics of each (I'm
not assuming a critic of one is a critic of all) think these cards aren't
flattening tables at every tournament only due to their rarity? That kind
of needs to be clear for this discussion to be in proper context.

This is true of so many Master Cards as to be ridiculous. Art Museum
gains you one pool, effectively, and so "costs 1". Next turn it "costs 0."
Minion tap costs "X blood and -X pool" where "X" is how much you take off.
AI isn't special at all in this sense.

> If you
> can play AI at all, you were losing more than three pool to a
> bleed. That "3" in the lower left corner isn't a "normal" cost,
> because the effect of the card will save you at least four pool.
> And if it's Sudden Reversed, you don't pay the 3 pool either.
> So: all that "3" does is define the minimum "swing" you gain by
> playing the card: at least 1 pool. If it were a 4, you would gain
> at least 0 pool by playing it; if it were a 2, you would gain at
> least 2 pool by playing it. As such, taking the effect of the
> card when played into consideration along with the printed "3"
> is just as reasonable and accurate as taking the effect of
> Ascendance (gain 1 pool) into consideration when discussing the
> costs and benefits of that card.
>
> Saying that AI costs 3 pool, while technically accurate, *does*
> ignore its effects, because if you can't pay the cost, you can't
> take the bleed either.

I have no argument with your logic. And, yes saying "AI costs 3 pool"
does ignore the effect. Partially I got annoyed at the metric of "negative
pool cost" when someone (Norm?) said "Given it's cost of 3 pool..." and
someone (you? someone else? I forget) jumped in with "It costs NEGATIVE
pool! Do I have to explain it again?" which just confuses the issue, instead
of addressing it. Had the response been more like "yes, but you can't
ignore..." and tacked on bits of your above paragraph, that would have been
productive. But the "negative cost" argument by itself as a sound byte only
misleads. Not by itself, a full explanation obviates the need for unclear
terms like "negative cost."

Put simpler:

> Saying that AI costs 3 pool, while technically accurate, *does*
> ignore its effects,

AND, saying "AI has a negative cost," is *neither* accurate *nor* does it
account for all its effects, so please don't answer the claim of the former
with the latter. Better yet, just be clear and avoid both
oversimplifications.

It's your best option if you're playing Setites. Other clans have other
options. You can have effective bleed defence in a Ventrue deck without
Deflection/Redirection, but it's going to be (by necessity) less
efficient, because you're choosing to neglect your best option.

Rush as combat defence, but you are, again, choosing to neglect your
best option. Which can make for some neat decks, mind you.

a substantial pool gainer. Legal Manipulations and Social Charm gain a pool
when played at superior. If you're gaining 2-3 pool a turn, _just for
doing what you'd do anyway_, it matters a bit less that you're bleeding
a tiny bit more slowly than the dominate decks.

I'm not bothered by having some clans favor some tactics. Setites favor
S&B -- so your best tourney option if you're dead set on playing Setites
is to play a Setite S&B deck, unless you've got crazy deck skill, play
skill, and are looking to make a point. Which is certianly possible.

turn?)...would the card still be used if it did this? Probably
not...but it produces a similar effect (cancels the bleed), and renders

of its flavor.

ever be used, even if the cost was reduced to 2 or so?

I'm pretty sure it wouldn't be, as even though it would still be
useful, people would be so dismayed that it no longer burns a vampire,
that they would resort to other methods of bleed defense where they
would have normally used AI.

What does this introduce to the argument? I'm not sure. I guess I'm
just trying to determine what people think the crux of the matter is.
I suspect that Josh, James, Peter, and I think that it is unreasonable
to be able to burn someone's vampire (reactively) for 3 pool. I am not
sure what Norm and Pat (and others?) think the problem (if there is
one) with AI is.

I think it comes down to the following questions:

Is bleed (as a strategy) overpowered?
Is AI's effect disproportionate to its cost? If so, is there any way
to make the cost-effect ratio proportionate?
Is AI an effective deterrent for large-bleed decks?

It all depends on what your answers to these questions are, I guess.
My answers would be yes, yes, maybe, and no.

Not to mention that for the cost of Zebulon you can get 2 or 3 effective
rushers. Obedience is indeed good, but to try to work that as a defensive
angle while going for large unblockable bleeds is tough, and more than
a little slow. And then there's the vulernability! As you point out below,
it's possible to win tournaments with unblockable bleed decks, but then
again I've heard of equipment or ally decks winning tournaments as well.

>> I've won a tournament with unblockable bleeds before. If you build your
>>deck around them, they're just not that hard to get off.
>
>I've been poking around with unblockables, and my experience is that
>the setup is so elaborate (whether you're using Day Op, Daring the Dawn,
>Horrific Countenance, or the vastly inferior Concoction of Vitality and
>Sunrise Service) that you HAVE to bleed for a lot in one bleed to make
>it worthwhile. Deflection already makes this strategy chancy -- AI makes
>it worthless.

The only way I was ever able to get millage out of "unblockable" bleeds
was with Grave Robbing. Large bleeds backed by drawing out the beast and
dawn op, with Form of Mist to get through. Then grave robbing and
stealth to steal those who end up in torpor. The crypt was a bit large,
and the deck didn't have much defense, but it was more reliable than I'd
expected. Not the most effective deck, but frightening to be in front of.

Of course, my friends and I never bought any of the VtES set, and so nobody
had access to Archon Investigation or Protected Resources -- which would
have completely shut the deck down.

My problem with AI and PR is that they target decks that aren't so great
to begin with, and do so not by weakening them, but by hosing them. Lame.
They throw several viable deck concepts out of the metagame, without adding
anything to balance -- since the real problem was (and is) weenie bleed,
which can both afford to lose it's cheap vampires, and doesn't need to make
big bleeds.

I don't think these cards are so much overpowered, as simply bad for the
game.
-Jasper

> >way
> > to make the cost-effect ratio proportionate?

Now we're getting somewhere...

> I think a valid problem with AI is it's "all or nothing" power.
> It's a balanced card (as it and big bleed are BOTH still played, but
> Big Bleed moreso than AI) but only in the "average" sense. If it
> works, it *really* fucks the guy, but if he never bleeds for more
> than 3, it's wallpaper.

I can't agree...a bleed for 4 just isn't that much. I might be a
little more okay with it if it was a bleed over 5 or something. As far
as I can tell, this card was originally developed to deal with 4CL S&B
and (fudging the release dates here, because I can't remember) RTI.

> Do people actually ABUSE Archon Investigation? If not, it seems
> a bit shaky ground to want to errata/ban the card.
>
> (forgive me if I repeat myself too much; I'm still waiting for people
> to tell me how much AI screws their playgroup/tournament/etc.)

I recently saw it burn Arika after she bled for some non-ungodly
amount, probably just bleed + Threats, or something...say 5. The
Methuselah who tossed it down was highly thrilled, as she had recently
had Miller, the Celerity Monkey burned by Arika's successful Protect
Thine Own. I still think it's inappropriate to burn a vampire just for
bleeding for 4 or 5...again, if the card either torporized the vampire
instead of burning it, or the bleed requirement was higher, I'd feel
better about the card, but as is, it's simply too easy to burn a
vampire that is bleeding for just 4 or so. I admit that I don't see it
played a lot, but most of the people I play with don't have much V:tES,
it's mainly Jyhad.

So, this is once again a case where I fail to come to a decisive
conclusion, as I certainly don't have the data to do so. I don't think
that there is widespread abuse of the card, as it is a reactive
strategy...however, I do think that the card is too powerful for its
cost...which justifies changing it, if it were reprinted.

And incidentally, I think it's pretty entertaining that we're getting
whipped up in such a froth at the *possibility* of these cards being
reprinted in an expansion, not due to certain knowledge that they'll be
in the expansion. :)

Messages.Body:
On Tue, 12 Dec 2000 15:08:22 -0600, James Hamblin
<ham...@math.wisc.edu> wrote:

>Derek Ray wrote:
>>
>> On Mon, 11 Dec 2000 22:02:12 -0600, James Hamblin
>> <ham...@math.wisc.edu> wrote:
>>
>> >It's not only the extremity of the punishment, but also the _negative_
>> >cost of the card. It costs you _negative_ pool, since you spend three
>> >pool to cancel a bleed of more than three. Oh, it costs you a master
>> >phase action, too. If the card didn't cancel the bleed, it would at
>> >least be more reasonable, if still unnecessary.
>>
>> (shrug) It costs you a slot in your deck,
>
>...just like every other card. This is a non-point.

It costs you a slot that doesn't easily 'move' for something else. If
you get it in your hand early on, it also costs you a hand slot while
you wait for someone to bleed for more than 3. If nobody bleeds you
for more than 3, then you have not only wasted a deck slot, you've
wasted a hand slot for several turns; hanging onto the card can be
very risky. If you discard it, you pretty much run up the "If you
have modifiers, smack me now" flag and wave it around.

>> hoping like hell you're
>> going to be bled for 4 at some point.
>
>I have agreed that the card is not _always_ useful. It's that _when_ it
>_is_ useful, it's _too_ useful.

It is undercosted, but not overuseful despite the undercost.

>> And you actually have to TAKE
>> the bleed for at least 3, instead of just arranging for some other
>> fashion to deal with it.
>
>Huh? You don't take the bleed. You lose 3 pool instead of the 4+ you
>were going to take, _and_ they lose their vampire.

You lose 3 pool. Correct. This is still taking pool damage from a
bleed. Instead of using AI, you could use cards that permit you to
take ZERO pool damage from a bleed, which you will have in your deck
ANYWAY to deal with bleeds of 3 or less. By your logic, this is a
gain of an ADDITIONAL 3 pool just for using other strategies besides
AI. But of course, you do not burn a vampire.

AI's cost is best stated as written: Pay 3 pool to burn a vampire who
just attempted to bleed you for more than 3. All the math juggling
and number sliding you are performing does not disguise the true cost
of the card: 3 pool, and the opportunity cost of having to have a
deck attempt to bleed you for 4 or more. The effect of the card:
Burn a vampire.

Let's look at the OTHER Master cards that effectively burn a vampire.

Fear of Mekhet, 2 pool, opportunity cost: find a Justicar or IC.
Vulnerability, 1 pool, oc: find a vampire in torpor.
Society of Leopold, free, oc: find an empty vampire.
Vicissitude Poisoning, free, oc: find a vamp using VIC lots.
Obsession, 2 pool, oc: find an empty !Toreador.
Out of Control, 2 pool, oc: find a !Brujah below 6.
Millicent Smith, free, oc: block a minion acting with Millicent.

To this we can add AI. So which of these cards are broken and deserve
banning? In my mind, only Out of Control really falls in the "get
lost!" pile, and THAT because its conditional is ridiculously
non-conditional. Anyone claiming the !Brujah are "too strong" is on
loony pills, whereas someone claiming that bleed is "too strong" has
at least a chance of making a coherent argument.

Also, I submit that having a vampire in torpor on someone else's
Master phase is almost as frequent as a vampire bleeding for more than
3. Vulnerability costs 2 less pool than AI. Is Vulnerability broken?

>> Why it was created isn't what I'm discussing; it's here now, and we're
>> stuck with it unless we ban it.
>
>I think this is relevant. If the reason for creating the card was that
>"bleed is too powerful", then we should address two points: (1) Before
>AI, was bleed too powerful? and (2) If so, does AI "fix" the problem?

as I mentioned in my response to Josh, (1) is self-evident from the
horror many people still feel in reaction to Malk S&B, or indeed, ANY
S&B. Bleed WAS too powerful. A lot of the "old timer" players we
pick up evince that same horror at seeing even a bleed at ONE stealth.

Did AI fix the problem? It provided a partial fix by slowing down the
amounts hit for on any given action, giving someone more time to
Minion Tap/Rush or use any of their other defenses. Elder
Intervention provided more of a "fix", in my mind, by providing easy
generic access to intercept; this meant that no longer was one Lost in
Crowds sufficient against everyone but the Toreador intercept decks
and the 2nd Tradition guys.

Did PR fix the problem? It provided another partial fix by slowing
down the amounts hit for. I doubt it saw much use.

>In his other posts, Norman seems to be arguing that bleed is _still_ too
>powerful, whereas I would say that bleed has never been too powerful.

(see above)

>> The question is, it is so unbalancing
>> that it needs to be banned? Or would banning it tip the scale too far
>> towards the bleed decks?
>
>Was the scale balanced toward bleed decks before AI was printed? I
>think not. If AI were banned, would everyone suddenly start playing
>crazy bleed decks? Probably not. There were and are plenty of ways to
>deal with bleed decks (and for the thousandth time, Norman, you don't
>have to have Dom or Aus).

See above. when AI was printed, it was just Jyhad. There were NOT as
many ways as there are currently.

>> If you Banish a 5-cap with 2 blood, it is effectively an unbounceable,
>> unreduceable bleed for 3 OR a total removal of a significant resource
>> (the vampire). EVEN IF it is only a bleed for 3, it is still a
>> TEMPORARY removal of that resource for a turn, which could be used to
>> defend against other bleeds or damage. It is far too overpowered for
>> the fact that Igo can call and pass it by himself.
>
>AI is too powerful when it can make you gain pool while at the same time
>burn any vampire. If there were some limitation (could only burn
>vampires with cap <= 3, say), then it would be more acceptable. But
>Arika getting burned for playing Bonding is ridiculous.

Again, AI does not make you gain pool. You lose 3 pool for playing
it. There is no "gain" involved. You could always block the bleed
and lose none. You could Deflect the bleed and lose none. Please
quit trying to bend the cost with semantics.

Arika getting burned IS difficult, yes, because her built-in +2 bleed
makes her most vulnerable. But IC members are difficult to deal with
anyway; the best solution I've seen in awhile is just to bring them
out, Minion Tap them down to 4, and treat them as 4-caps with a lot of
toys. I don't mind an Arika who cost me 4 getting burned as much as I
mind a full Arika getting burned.

I wouldn't mind seeing AI be unable to target IC members or Justicars,
myself; that suitably restricts an Archon's imaginary function without
making the card pointless. (sure, you can make Ozmo the Malk Justicar
with a vote, but that's an awful lot of trouble to go to just to give
the boy immunity to AI.)

>> >But not unbalancingly strong. Since it wins in the most direct manner
>> >possible (removing prey's pool), it will of course be an effective deck
>> >type. But it is weak against combat, bleed bounce, bloat, intercept,
>> >etc.
>>
>> Bleed does not NEED to be weak against combat, bloat, OR intercept,
>> however; the trick lies in the deck construction.
>
>No matter how you build your deck, it will either have lots of defenses
>and not be especially good at accomplishing its primary goal (what I
>would call a "toolbox" deck), or be very focuced and have a vital
>vulnerability.

Again, read my post to Josh Duffin. It becomes very
rock-scissors-paper, and the bleed deck has the advantage.

>> A Ventrue/!Ventrue
>> DOM/FOR bleed deck is not vulnerable to combat.
>
>But it is vulnerable to light intercept.

Actually, I wouldn't even consider using stealth in such a deck. I
would use Seduction and Dawn Op instead, and let the intercept decks
jam up on their intercept cards.

>> A weenie Dominate
>> horde will overrun Minion Tap/5th.
>
>But will die to light intercept and combat.

Darn shame, that. (i have no sympathy for weenie dominate)

>> Malk S&B will beat intercept.
>
>But will be beaten by combat and/or some (heavy) intercept decks.

+3 intercept is rare to find in a tournament. But the original point
still stands; as things are now, you are safest playing bleed bounce.
AI helps you if you choose NOT to play bleed bounce, in a way that few
other cards can.

>[snip]
>> Do I want to see it banned since it got
>> here anyway? ...No.
>
>Is that because you are generally against banning, or because you have
>reasons for wanting it to stay?

I am, in fact, generally against banning until it's shown to be REALLY
necessary. Cards like RtI need to be shot on the spot and the
designer sacrificed. Madness of the Bard and Monocle of Clarity are
less obvious, but arguments have been put forth that show that it's
REALLY necessary that those be gone. I could care less about Rowan
Ring; if it came back I wouldn't bat an eye. And the Ante cards might
as well be gone.

I am much more in favor of errata... but again, only if a card is that
much of a problem. I don't see AI causing a problem.

>> >It's not the effectiveness of PR that makes me spew smoke from my ears
>> >when I see one. It's that its effect outweighs its cost dramatically.
>> >It's that it is impossible to get rid of; it almost requires a bleed
>>
>> This is true. Does that effect affect the game significantly, though?
>
>If I'm playing a bleed deck and my prey plays one, then it affects
>_that_ game significantly. The effect (depending on my deck) can be
>crippling, with very minimal cost.

Well; think of it this way. You probably have Govern + Bonding, or
Social + Aire in your hand. Now you just get to play them separately,
and you won't ever worry about running out of bleed cards, will you?
Short of actions? Relying on One Big Vampire to do it all is very bad
for any number of reasons, offense OR defense; I try to have at least
3 minions for any given game. Sure, your Govern + Bonding gets
reduced to 2 instead of 4. But 2 at a time still adds up... you just
get slowed down a bit.

>> >deck to pack Sudden Reversal just to prevent the card from ever getting
>> >played. I think it is only the relative scarcity of AI and PR that keep
>> >people from seeing them as the horribly unbalanced cards that they are.
>>
>> AI isn't scarce.
>
>RELATIVE scarcity. <sigh>

Relative to what, Deflection? It's not scarce; why use the word? PR
is scarce, mostly because of its extremely limited deck scope.

Do you see more than one in a deck? Nope. Why do you think that is?
Probably because that's too many deck slots to waste on a hope that
someone is going to try to get you for more than 3, that's why. And
you still have to use deck space defending against the bleeds for 3 or
less even WITH the Archons.

>> mondo-bleeders... that it's just not that good an inclusion in most
>> decks.
>
>I don't dispute these points. It's that when it does come out in the
>worst possible circumstances, there is no defense. There's no way to

Some days, you sit next to the deck that fucks you. This is how a
well-built stealth bleed deck feels when it sits behind Rush combat;
it knows that its grandpredator just got two free VPs. This is how
the Ventrue Law Firm feels when it sits next to the Tzimisce. Bad
luck happens.

>get rid of it, short of Sudden Reversal. _That's_ what should be
>fixed. As I suggested in another post, making the card a Unique
>Location would mostly appease me; at least there would be ways to deal
>with it.

If you make it a location, you make it worthless; now a simple Arson
removes your bleed defense, and you STILL can't bleed. I wouldn't
EVER use the thing. It is inherently limited sufficiently, and its
frequency of use indicates that its limitations are quite adequate.

-- Derek
Jack-Booted Thug of Atlanta

Messages.Author: Peter D Bakija

Norman wrote:
>>Couldn't another vampire that you brought into your controlled region
during your last turn block and play Obedience. Maybe someone like ,
Roland Bishop, Laurent de Valois, or Guido Lucciano .>>

Yup, they could. But then they weren't bleeding you last turn, and thus are
slower. Obediance is trouble to a Rush deck, sure, but how many Obediances are
they packing? How many are going to jam their hand when they aren't facing a
Rush deck? When you build a deck, you need to take into account *all* possible
decks you might face,and sure, you can put in enough Obediances to shut down
any Rush deck in the world, but doing so will kill you if you happen to sit
next to a non Rush deck. Thus, you need to balance the likelyhood of sitting
next to a Rush deck with how many Obediances you can afford to put in. In most
cases, the answer is "not many".

>>Don't need that much stealth just needs a little and a few seductions to
get past the guy with the permanent intercept.>>

And then if you sit next to a serious intercept deck, you get screwed. A deck
simply can't do *everything* it wants. If you guess right, and always end up
int he right seat, you'll win and deserve too.

>>could it be possible that the methuselah would actually transfer out
another vampire? This new vampire would be untapped and could block
and play reaction and combat cards to foil a rush deck.>>

Of course this is *possible*, but is it likely (not the transfering out the
other vampire, but having the combat cards *and* the ability to bleed for 7
consisitently)? Not really. Keeping this under the eye of the AI disucssion, I
have honestly never run into a deck in a tournament that had *both* enough
combat defense to shut down my Rush deck *and* the ability to bleed for 7
consistiently (and thus be succeptible to AI). All the S+B decks I have run
into in a tournament setting were either A) Capable of bleeding for 7
consistiently and had only limited combat defense or B) Has consistient combat
defense, but only bled for about 3 per action, at which point AI isn't an
issue.

>>I would argue that point. 10 GTu's and 10 Conditionings have the making
of a strong power bleed deck. Now throw in 10 Threats. That leave 60
cards to play with.>>

Ok. Of those 60 cards, 18-20 will be master cards, leaving ~40. Now add in
enough stealth so that you aren't stopped by light/permanent intercept (~15
cards, minimum), leaving ~25. Then add your own bleed defense (bounce?), about
8 cards, leaving you ~17. Add enough wakes so you can use the Bounce and any
Obediances you have (8?), leaving you 9-12 card slots for your Obediances, Fake
outs, and Dodges. And then you have a deck that is shut down by a heavy
intercept deck (as you only have minimum stealth), has no vote defense
whatsoever, and has only light combat defense, at best. Again, you can't do
everything at once.

>>So what is your point? If they can only bleed reliably for three, then
they don't even have to worry about Archon Investigation and it just
jams up their preys hand.>>

That you seem to be implying that AI is a viable counter to weenie bleed decks,
and weenie bleed decks are completely unhindered by AI.

Messages.Author: Peter D Bakija
Messages.Body:
Norman wrote:
>>AI doesn't hose bleeding as a strategy.>>

It is a hoser--it kills you just for showing up. If you have the audacity to
play Govern and Conditioning at the same time (even at inferior), you get a
vampire burned. If the game designers had an issue with bleeding as a strategy,
they should have taken a different route than the Magic Bullet that is AI.
Elder Intervention is a much more eloquent tweak to combat bleeding. AI is
simply too much.

>>It hoses bleeding for more than three, once. You only have to worry about
this card if you attempt to bleed for more than 10% of each methuselah's
starting pool. It is not a "shoddy strategy hoser" unless your strategy is
power bleeds.>>

And power bleeds is a perfectly valid strategy--AI hoses this strategy. If you
are playing a power bleeds deck, you get killed just for showing up. This is
not good, as there were already (pre AI) plenty of viable defenses against
Power Bleeding. AI was unecessary and simply lazy.

>>It is no more a hoser on a per cost basis than a bounce.>>

Bounce does not burn a vampire.

>>A bleed deck should pack a little combat defence. Usually Obediences or
Fake Outs and Dodges do the trick.>>

Again, if you have enough Obediance, Fake Outs, and Dodges to reliably survive,
your deck is going to be *much* slower and much less effective.

>>So all these strategies make AI broken? How?>>

No, no. They make AI unecessary. AI makes AI broken. It is a card that the game
did not need. It is a trump card. A stratgey hoser. It punishes a very common
and effective strategy simply for being played. If the designers had trouble
with the power of bleeding, they should have found better, more subtle ways
than the sledgehammer that is AI.

>>How does this scenario sound? You are going first in a four player
game. Your lowest vamp in your uncontrolled region is a six. You put
one pool on him. Your predator plays either a Dreams of the Sphinx or a
Info Highway. He then puts into play Royce, Ohanna, and Christine
Bocasci. On your turn you play the Barrens and transfer 4 more pool,
still not getting a vampire out. Your predator plays a Dominate skill
card on Royce. Royce Governs the Unaligned with Threats for 6. Ohanna
Governs the Unaligned with Conditioning for 6. Christine Bocasci
Governs the Unaligned wtih Conditioninf for 6. You just lost 18 pool on
turn two. You now have 7 Pool and 5 on a uncontrolled six cap vampire.>>

Sounds like I am playing the wrong deck in an environment where I should have
been expecting (and thus planning on) weenie bleed decks.

>>What about the Followers of Set?>>

They are basically screwed. The answer is that the Followers of Set need more
cards that help the combat bleeds, not that they need AI. Followers of Set are
just as screwed against a speedy bleed deck that only bleeds for 3 an action,
and AI isn't going to help them at all there.

>>The only defense currently availible in this scenario is a Archon
Investigation, which still costs you three pool to play.>>

No, the best defense is not to go into a tournament where you expect to face
weenie bleed decks with a deck that will get itself in this situation. I also
fail to see how AI will even help--how many do you have in your deck? 1? 6? In
the situation you present above, is playing a single AI even going to save you?
No, you are going to die anyway.

>>Your predator has lost a disposable weenie. You would be down to 10 pool
with 5 on a uncontrolled six cap. How is Archon Investigation broken in this
scenario?>>

AI is broken because its effect (burn a vampire and net you a gain in pool) is
out of proportion to its cost (a master phase).

ban

That's not exactly what I was getting at, no. My point was that
out of seventy-three tourney-winning decks, only 13 had AI in
them - this seems to indicate that AI is *not* the only plausible
way to defend against bleed and win tournaments. Also, that many
decks using AI also used bounce; to me this suggests that these
players were particularly paranoid about bleed. Not necessarily
that they should have been, but that they were.

Going back through the list and counting up the decks with
bounce in them (decks with at least 4 of Deflection, Redirection,
Telepathic Misdirection, or any combination), 44 of 73 had some
bounce. A much higher percentage, yes, but that leaves 29 of
73 (39.7%) with absolutely no (or an insignificant proportion)
of bounce. There would be four of those that had a single AI
in them, but the other 25 won tournaments without any bounce
or AI defense against bleeds. To me that suggests that AI is
not necessary (and therefore excessive - since I object to the
extreme effect of AI when played, what I'm trying to show is
that, since the strategy it hoses is not overpowered, it should
not exist).

> I never argued that "it must be the only way to win tournaments -
ie
> it was necessary to keep the bleeders from always killing you." I
> argued that it wasn't powerful enough or unbalancing enough to require
> either banning or errata.

I'm not even sure that it *is* so very powerful (ie makes you
win lots of games) to require banning. But I do think it's that
unbalancing. The basic problem I have with the card is that its
design is Just Plain Brown Wrong. Burning a vampire as an OOT
master is Not An Appropriate Mechanic. (Burning a vampire through
any means except diablerie or excess agg damage is, to my mind,
a Big Deal and should be examined Very Closely.)

and elsewhere (combining two posts into one...):

In article <915tfi$t0n$1...@nnrp1.deja.com>,
X_Ze...@email.msn.com wrote:
>
> I don't believe that bleed cards are broken or for that matter that
any
> of the cards in the current Sabbat War Set or errata are broken.
> The tournament banned cards are the ones I don't play with so I
> really don't have an opinion on them. Certainly you must realize that
> bleeding is the most efficient manner in which to oust your prey.
Power
> -bleeds are just an extention of that strategy. I think that Archon
> Investigation is a appropriate response in both terms of Card Balance
> and Storyline. I don't think AI is broken, nor do I think that
> power-bleeding is broken. I believe that they actually balance one
> another even in the presence of other bleed defense.

Yes, bleeding *is* the most direct route toward ousting your
prey. I wrote a little about that in another post in this thread,
I think. But that doesn't mean it needs to have hosers out of
all proportion to the rest of the game. There aren't any OOT
masters that say "Play when a vampire attempts to do more than 3
damage in a single strike to one of your minions. Burn that
vampire." because it would be absurd. There aren't any OOT masters
that say "Play when a vampire calls a referendum that passes by
more than 3 votes. Burn that vampire." because it would be absurd.
There shouldn't be an OOT master that says "Play when a vampire
attempts to bleed you for more than 3 pool. Burn that vampire."
because it is absurd. Unfortunately, that card *does* exist. But
it shouldn't. That's what I'm trying to get across. It doesn't
belong in this game any more than pre-errata Thoughts Betrayed did.

Josh

> know what? If you're moving along and dropping multiple big bleeds
> and get a minion burned, yeah it slows you down, but it's probably not
> going to stop you cold unless you're doing the "Etrius bleeds for 10!"
> stunt or something. I know that if I build a bleed deck, I will
> deliberately ignore one of the defense types; usually I'll include
> combat defense and plenty of bleed oomph, and go a little lighter on
> the stealth, as most people are well aware of the "don't block them"
> theory regarding stealth/bleed. I hate getting caught behind a Minion
> Tap for 10, and getting my minions beat up is never a good thing. And
> I also ignore the threat of Archon Investigation. Sure, someone will
> drop it on me eventually. I just try not to make any given minion
> that much 'better' than any other. It happened in my Tzimisce
> Pulse/Changeling deck; I had 3 Pulsed guys out and made the mistake of

> and poof. The deck still got 3 VP that game.

My objection isn't so much that AI will burn every vampire a
large-bleed deck plays (although it could), but that every time
AI is played its effect is too large for its cost. It is, thus,
overpowered, and cards have been errataed for less. (cough, Immortal
Grapple, cough ;-)

your prey's pool to zero. Nothing, but NOTHING, does that better than

as offended by a single bleed of 8 a turn than I am by 3 bleeds of 5. For
numerically obvious reasons. And, yes, AI does discourage the former more
than the latter. But, there are far more pressing reasons that "big"
vampire decks don't work. They come out slower, and take less actions.

Bum's Rush torporization by a dedicated combat deck fucks your deck as bad
or as little as the AI. Don't make AI the bogeyman when the issue is that
picking large vamps is, without sound reasoning, a boneheaded thing to do in
