wrote:

>In article <B65D5FEB.15A1%sp...@socrates.gatech.edu>,
>Pat Ricochet <sp...@socrates.gatech.edu> wrote:
>>> I don't know about that...the Jyhad designers obviously didn't, but I
>>> think there's a whole lot of supposition that V:tES was rewritten by
>>> people that were either playing with a very limited card pool, or were
>>> playing 4CL. Why AI, Justicar Retribution, Protected Resources, Elder
>>> Intervention, and not some more vote or combat defense?
>>
>> Well, because likely, then, as now, combat didn't win, and vote was
>>already pretty counterable (DT, Surprise Influence, Dread Gaze, etc.). It
>>was bleed that you had to work too damn hard to avoid, unless you could
>>bounce the bleed. Probably, Malk S&B won over and over. They just gave
>>bleed defense to everyone.
>
>Which is exactly the argument being presented. Malk S&B would only win
>over and over again with either a limited card set, or a 4CL. S&B honestly
>isn't that effective of a strategy, as it is so easy to counter, in a variety
>of different ways.

It's not whether it WOULD win, it's whether it DID win. Remember that
we are talking about 1995-1996 here; strategy in general had not
evolved to the point it has today. Again, the horror and disgust that
old-time Jyhad players will evince when you play Malk S&B demonstrates
that there certainly WAS a problem. Partly, it was a strategy
shortage; the Malks were the most obvious. Partly, it was a card
shortfall; Elder Intervention and Pack Tactics didn't exist, and a lot
of the weenie-AUS vampires also did not exist yet, making Telepathic
Misdirection a much more ineffective tool for bounce. The V:TES
printing was the second thing off of WotC's shelves for this game.

Interestingly, the cheapest vampires who could bounce with AUS were:

Dorian Strack, Aleph (4): Torie and Malk
Felicia Mostrom (5): Torie
Kallista, Dancin' Dana, Ozmo (6): Torie and Malk

So if you were playing the Malk bleeders, you had THAT advantage too -
a combination intercept and bounce card, as necessary. The Toreador
weren't helpless, but certainly were very limited.

There was no superior Dominate below 5; it was Didi Meyers or nothing.
There were some cheap weenie Dominate vampires, but a lot of those
were Malkavian too.

There was no suitable Dominate on the Brujah, Nosferatu, or Gangrel -
leaving three clans TOTALLY without access to bounce and two of those
without any real access to intercept. Now factor in Obedience being
found on the Malks, a few Disguised .44s or just Zip Gun and Behind
Yous, and we can see very quickly how Malk S&B was a real monster back
then. Many of the defenses everyone likes to quote didn't exist yet.

>In particular combat can win -- particularily against S&B, and votes
>are no more counterable than S&B bleed.

But AI and PR came into the set for some very good reasons, frankly.

With regards to the other statement above; one bleed of 3 at 1 stealth
is THE simplest and most effective means to reduce pool in the entire
game, bar none. It can be pulled off with two cards and two
disciplines in multiple different forms. It can be pulled off with
permanents in multiple forms. It can be pulled off with a combination
of the two.

It is not surprising that a vote deck's inherent unit of damage also
happens to be 3 pool at 1 stealth; the weaknesses of vote compared to
bleed is that two players instead of one may block, and the entire
table has a say in whether the vote passes or not.

This is why bleed is superior to vote; sure, you can Deflect a bleed,
but the onus is still entirely on you and your deck, and you will run
out of Deflections eventually. It is easier to produce multiple
bleeds of 3 at 1 stealth than it is to produce Deflections. You can
also generate intercept, but simply blocking and punching each minion
is not enough; you must do something to them as well, or they will
simply come over again next turn with the same stuff; and they have
more of it than you have intercept, unless your deck does nothing but
intercept backwards (a failing deck). You can also Rush the minions,
but with a Rush deck you also must figure out how to oust the rest of
the non-S&B table, even assuming you get the S&B deck. Not all S&B
decks fail to include combat defense, by the way.

It is far more complicated to PROPERLY defend against bleed than it is
to generate bleed, and this is why bleed remains THE superior
strategy; although far less than it was before the expansions. It is
worth noting that bleed is the only cardless action of the "big three"
strategies.

It's also worth noting that AI and PR don't even slow down this
strategy. This is part of the reason the strategy is so strong;
attempts to move faster are more vulnerable to Deflection and AI/PR.
Both of these keep bleed decks in check, or you might find that they
were even stronger than you thought.

>><opinion>
>> I think the ideal that "combat, vote, and bleed" are the 3 Core
>>Strategies that are somehow balanced is a big load of bunk. They all have
>>checks and balances against each other, but you don't win unless you reduce
>>your prey's pool to zero. Nothing, but NOTHING, does that better than
>>bleed.
>></opinion> (only stressed here because we can go in circles on THAT forever
>>and ever, and already have; it's somewhat beside the point)
>
>Shrug. Voting decks tend to have other cool effects that are just as good,
>for example banishment, table rearrangement, and pool gain. Combat decks
>may not bleed the fastest, but how fast can your predator bleed with
>no ready minions?

At that point, it's how fast your grand-predator can bleed, and then
you have to get rid of HIS minions. Being forced to vaporize all your
predator's minions is almost always a losing situation for the Rush
deck, as it doesn't get the breathing room it needs and was looking
for to go forward.

Vote decks are strong, yes, but the entire table has an interest in
prohibiting the vote deck from gaining a VP, if only because a VP
gained by the vote deck is not a VP they can gain. When it comes down
to it, if it's them or you, it's going to be them, and a vote deck
that's been passing votes by alliance will suddenly dry up and wither
away unless it has an alternative.

>I definitely don't see bleeding as being the strongest strategy.

Keep looking, then; and consider how strong a WELL built S&B (in any
appropriate clan, or out of) can be, not the stupid "10 Govern, 10
Condition, 8 Lost, 8 Faceless" Malk S&B that everyone holds up as a
straw man to shoot at.

Messages.Author: James Coupe
Messages.Body:
In article <918puu$aot$1...@nnrp1.deja.com>, Xian <xi...@waste.org> writes

>I don't know about that...the Jyhad designers obviously didn't, but I
>think there's a whole lot of supposition that V:tES was rewritten by
>people that were either playing with a very limited card pool, or were
>playing 4CL. Why AI, Justicar Retribution, Protected Resources, Elder
>Intervention, and not some more vote or combat defense?

Because, I would assert, at the time the bleed deck archetype was the
strongest of the triumvirate.

Today's lesson is taken from the Book of Ooi, Chapter 10:

***

In the beginning was the bleed. 'Twas the one that most players tended
to "see" first, when exercising their newly bestowed brains. It was
there, it was quick, it was simple. It had flaws, yet the power of the
Sleaze was too much for the newbies to resist.

And thus was the stealth and bleed deck well explored. "Commandment
One: Bleed fast, bleed hard, kill, kill, kill." The vote archetype was
somewhat less well endowed with exploration. With each clan being
somewhat restricted in its voting due to lack of Princes etc. in most
cases, vote decks were a somewhat more risky prospect. Playing weenie
vote was also all about dumping your entire hand onto the table, rather
than permanent votes, and so it tended to empty itself quickly.

And combat was a different kettle of (loaves and) fish(es) altogether.
Damn fun to play - always has been - but S:CE tended to crop up rather a
lot in the form of Majesty, a card which players quickly understood and
explored. Immortal Grapple in large quantities was generally not seen -
*partly* because people like PDB6 etc. who were to pioneer the Immortal
Grapple rush strategies were playing with xCL.

Yea, the Designers did look upon the landscape and saw that it was bad.
In their mercy, they did smite the unholy Malkavians and their sneaky
brethren by creating the Cards of Holiness. Lo, it was good.

Then Time begat Knowledge, and Knowledge begat Skill. Time also begat
Playing and Playing begat Innovation. Then Skill and Innovation were
bound together in blissful union, and the old barren land was made
fertile once more.

Voting was ploughed up and begat its bastard child, the Weenie
Presence/Praxis Seizure Deck. And Combat was alike restored to its full
heavenly virtue, being powered by the skills of the Immortals.

And verily, Bleed did covet its neighbours ox and did play with Combat,
and thus was Bruise and Bleed begat. And in their new found Virtue,
Voting and Combat did unite, sharing the love of Cousins (probably in
the Deep South somewhere), and thus was Bruise and Vote found.

And lo, it was good.

Then, as people forgot their virtue and returned to the worship of the
Golden Cheese, they found that the designers had indeed messed it up,
that bleed could now be combated by the new virtues of Combat and
Voting, and the unions created thereby. Sadness fell upon the land as
they realised the folly of their Creators, cursing the day that Justicar
Retribution was ever created, or Moses for bringing down the Eleventh
Commandment "Thou shalt protect thy race-horses." The love of law and
order was likewise chastised as people realised that they would, verily,
rather get ripped off than have to suffer police protection, in the form
of "Ah! Con Investigation".

And PDB6 wept.

Yet, as time passed, the Designers' Folly, as 'twas henceforth known,
was lost amongst the mists of time and became subsumed in amongst the
evolution of the New Ways. And verily, no-one dared spake of the
Designers' Folly, save for in hushed tones, just in case someone did try
to do nasty things with them.

***

Here endeth the lesson.

presence of AI encourages deck diversity and allows people to play clans

know it sucks to have one of your vampires burned when you are "going
for the gusto", but to avoid it all you have to exert is a little
self-control and not bleed for more than 3.

all it was good for was burning people who Governed and added
a +bleed mod or who had a Pulse and added a +bleed. That the

were fairly clueless as to what the most effective strategies
really were.

There were nine princes in Jyhad, capacities of 1x6, 4x7, 3x8,

is not significant. It looks to me like vote was better than
bleed in Jyhad.

people really started playing bloat decks until much later. In
that respect I think James Coupe's quotation from the Book of Ooi
may have some accuracy - no one really knew that clearly what
they were doing, back then, and the VTES designers really jumped
the gun in printing such absurd cards so soon after the initial
release.

Meyers, and Ozmo are still the core of any Malk S&B deck, and well
they should be; they all come with the basic two disciplines
necessary. Add two Obfuscate skill cards and two Dominate skill

(Or you can add 1x Gilbert and 1x Mariel, Lady Latex)

inferior OBF/DOM is almost as good as superior. Govern is still 3 at
inferior, and Conditioning is still an extra +2, and against the
Brujah and Nosferatu, you just needed to have 1 stealth, 2 at the

Cloak. Bleeds of either 3 or 5, at stealth, consistently. Add a
Hunting Ground so your guys have a little blood gain back onto them,

OBF stealth. Scouting Mission and Foreshadowing Destruction merely
made it a bit easier for the DOM bleed decks to go; but they were fine
beforehand.

timetable. Your prey will always be there until YOU do something
about them. But if you're relying on AUS to bleed-bounce, or trying

overpowered. Consider the hypothetical card: "Reaction. Play
when another Methuselah's vampire plays Immortal Grapple. Burn
that vampire and gain ten pool." Is this card overpowered for
its cost (0 blood and a cardslot)? Yes. But can you build a

similar for AI. ;-)

no repeat actions part came up. They were some of the first winning

Tenets in the first place, and probably has a better idea of what

<X_Ze...@email.msn.com> wrote in message news:91aj20$mqm$1...@nnrp1.deja.com...

> I agree that there are other methods to deal with big bleed, but I don't
> believe that AI is inherently broken or overpowered. I certainly don't
> think that because AI doesn't work on every bleed that it should be
> banned because it it a corner case card.

AI isn't a "corner case" card. Foreshadowing Destruction is a corner case
card. Twisting the Knife is a corner case card (albeit a shitty one). Psyche
is a corner case card.

Unless I have been misunderstanding the usage all along, I have understood
"corner case" to mean a card that has a similar use to another card, but is
only *more* useful in specific circumstances (the corner case).

AI isn't always useful. However, it is *unprecedented* in its ability to
outright burn a vampire. There aren't any other cards that do this in any
similar manner. All of the master cards that have been brought up
(Vulnerability, Out of Control) require specific circumstances...Vulnerability
all but requires that the vampire it burns sucks at combat...Out of Control,
while *only* burning a !Brujah of less than 6 capacity, is seen by at least
some players as far too powerful for a clan hoser. I can't think of another
hoser card that is this powerful. Sure, Malkavian Dementia, in combination
with, say, Anson/Rumors/Parthenon could grab someone else's Malkavian and
Golconda it, but that's still pretty iffy...you're an idiot if you design a
deck around it, and you're lucky if you can pull it off more than once in a
game.

AI is too powerful for its cost.

> > Come *on* Norm, let's encourage diversity. Let the fools play with
> their 8+
> > bleed monsters, and then show them why it's Just A Bad Idea (tm).
>
> Are you saying that everybody uses AI, and that it is a mainstay for all
> decks? I would argue that it is not a mainstay for all decks. I would

I was by no means saying that. What I meant was, yes, big bleed decks might
win some games if AI isn't around. That doesn't mean that big bleed decks
shouldn't win games. In fact, big bleed decks should win some games, just to
reward the people that play them. Accept that, given the right circumstances,
any (reasonably well-constructed) deck is going to win at least 1 VP at some
point...so big bleed decks should. However, very, very, very often, big bleed
decks are going to run into something that they can't deal with (combat,
bounce, whatever)...but AI should not punish them for bringing it to the table
in the first place.

> No offense Xian, but I think that it would be a little risky to use your
> +2 bleeder to try and draw the block and then push it to a +3 bleed with

Actually, I'd probably be trying to draw it with Arika using a GtU or Scouting
Mission. But I agree that it's foolish to toss down the stealth and expect
the block.

> bonding for the stealth and still be expecting to draw the block.
> Maybe, it could happen, but I still don't think that your gambit of
> trying to draw out a block with a Inner Circle Member with bonding is a
> valid reason to change AI.

No, it is not, in and of itself, a valid reason to change AI. I was just
trying to offer an example of a situation where AI is toasting vampires all
out of proportion to what it should be doing.

> AI does punish most harshly those decks that can least recover from the
> loss of a minion. So does rush, and so does banishment. Unlike rush and

Ah, but rush can be defended against, as can banishment.

> banishment, you can avoid AI by simply not bleeding for more than 3. I

Again, AI is punishing you for bringing your deck to the table. I don't see
why I should be forced to stop playing a particular deck style (big vampire
tap-n-bleed, specifically) just because AI so completely screws it.
Banishment and Rush can be defended against by the minions, but the only
defense against AI is either a cross-table SR, or bleeding out-of-turn, and
SRing it yourself. Rush & Banishment can be prepared for without altering
your deck concept, and including a simple defense. AI cannot be prepared for
without *fundamentally* altering your deck concept.

> know it sucks to have one of your vampires burned when you are "going
> for the gusto", but to avoid it all you have to exert is a little
> self-control and not bleed for more than 3.

Jyhad is a game of excess isn't it? :) Self-control sucks ass.

Messages.Author: wes
Messages.Body:
I was playing when the game first came out... although my friends and I
played quite badly to be honest. However, I think I can shed some light on
some of your questions, at least as far as the games I saw back then...

> >"Derek Ray" <lor...@yahoo.com> wrote in message
> >news:u9eg3tc28posqkbec...@4ax.com...
> >> There was no suitable Dominate on the Brujah, Nosferatu, or Gangrel -
> >> leaving three clans TOTALLY without access to bounce and two of those
> >> without any real access to intercept. Now factor in Obedience being

Brujah were never seen as a viable clan in my group... there was a lot more
stealth and intercept and NO rush to speak of. Intercept of some variety was
not only nice but REQUIRED. At least the Nossies and Gangrel had access to
some with Raven Spies... and those were sure to show up in any Animalism
based deck. Brujah's ONLY real options were Sport Bikes (most common), Mr.
Winthrop and KRCG... plus the 2nd Tradition. Also, Potence was never seen as
a great discipline as it was limited to only one aspect of the game, ie.
combat, and useless for all other aspects. Although combat did occur, it was
not as brutal as it is now... at least not when compared to the vote and
bleed decks. Celerity was more common than Potence, most likely because guns
were also more common.

> >
> >Which two? I can only see the Brujah as without access to intercept.
The
> >Nosferatu and Gangrel as equally capable of intercepting, with their
> >Animalism. The Nosferatu even have one more minion with access to the
2nd
> >Tradition than the Gangrel do.
>
> The Nosferatu could only do it with Raven Spies though, because they
> didn't get ANI until a 7-cap. Even the Gangrel didn't get it until a
> 5-cap, but at least they could Freak Drive after getting a Raven Spy
> and have Cat's Guidance available to get to the +2 intercept you need
> as a BARE MINIMUM to hold up against stealth bleed. If they went more
> stealthy, you were screwed; +3 intercept just wasn't available early
> enough on in the game for the ANI guys.

Gangrel were preferable to the Brujah for combat simply due to aggravated
hand strikes which were seen as a LOT more effective than large hand
strikes... though in retrospect I can't see why. I guess it was more fun to
send them to torpor and make sure they don't get back out... Animilism was
used more for intercepts and untaps than it was for combat... there were not
nearly as many ANI combat cards as there are now... no Carrion Crows, no
Song in the Dark. Murder of Crows and Wolf Companion were there but not used
as often. Raven Spy would have been much more preferable. Also, because both
Gangrel and Nosferatu were lacking in blocking ability with say Auspex they
basically HAD to rely on Animilasm for their blocking. Staying untapped with
something like Freak Drive did not matter much when your minions had no
permanent intercept on them....

> As Josh said, Minion Tap/5th hadn't really entered play yet, and so I
> suspect that 2nd Tradition wasn't really making itself known these
> days as it is now; available to EVERYONE. People picked up the
> Nosferatu, saw "stealth and combat", and went that route with them.
> They picked up the Gangrel, saw all that ANI and all those ANI
> retainers, and went "intercept/agg combat" or just plain agg combat.

Actually, Minion Tap/5th Tradition was quite a healthy concept though the
5th was likely to be intercepted.

> >> But AI and PR came into the set for some very good reasons, frankly.
> >
> >No, they came in prematurely, without enough playtesting or thought, if
you
> >ask me.
>
> But how badly was S&B dominating things at the time? They were
> undoubtedly scared of losing players due to an accidental "bad
> imbalance" they had created; so they went for the fast fix with the
> reprint.

For our group, Malkavian Sneak and Bleed decks were completely dominant to
the point that they were boring as hell to play against. In fact, I would go
as far as to say that a lot of my friends probably stopped playing just
because they were sick of going up against Malk S&B decks. Even if you
played with something other than Malk S&B, you were forced to take them into
consideration... big time. At the time, I would definitely say that they
were a 'broken' concept... and for a while I think Archon Investigation did
an honest job of keeping them in their place... I remember keeping AI's in
my hand just to make them less eager to bleed... though again in retrospect
I think this was a bad idea. Effectively limiting yourself to a six-card
hand is not a great idea... but then none of us were 'great' players.

The game was VERY different than it is now... and not just the game, but the
community itself. For one thing, right now there IS a community! I mean,
only a few of us had any access to the Internet and no matter what rules
WotC was making after the fact, most of us did not know about them. There
may very well have been tournaments going on but I never knew of any... I
don't know if this NG existed back then, but again most of us would not have
known about it. Also, Jyhad was probably one of the first CCGs... I think
only a few other CCGs came between M:tCH and Jyhad that I can think of...
and I remember it being rather easy to convince Magic players to give Jyhad
a try... unlike today when I believe most players are afraid to play outside
of their ONE game... there must be three hundred CCGs or so... and nobody
wants to invest in a game that nobody will play with them. Back then, this
was not such a problem...

A lot of the strategies that this newsgroup takes for granted were simply
not around yet... or at least undiscovered. Immortal Grapple was always an
option but I don't remember ever seeing it as one. Rush decks themselves
were rarely thought of.... I remember making one and abandoning it after one
play. Weenie decks were around but not as 'weenie-ish' due to less small
capacity vampires to play with. Vote decks were powerful definitely... but
also hard to play with due to the amount of intercept on the table. Also, if
I recall correctly, most vote cards were rare... which limited them at least
in our group.

I find it quite amusing how many aspects of the game I have recently
discovered just by reading posts on this newsgroup... Although I for one
never grew bored with Jyhad, I find myself getting excited by the prospect
of playing again... especially with new cards! I attribute this mostly to
the innovative strategies I have seen here and the prospect of new players
with White Wolf's re-issue of the game. I've even signed up to play in JOL
148.

Hope this helps
WES

Messages.Author: Frederick Scott

"Andrew S. Davidson" wrote:
> I played Thoughts Betrayed in a game tonight and Tom said that it had
> errata. I wasn't having any of that and, looking at the details, am
> amazed - why make the card a coaster? No wonder the 7/7 errata were
> controversial if there's stuff like that in there.

It's real simple: your assumption is erroneous. The card, as errataed,
is not a coaster. Far from it, it's one of the most useful combat
cards in the game. Only thing is, you don't see it much because
its most useful function (now) is to prevent S:CE. And you don't see
a lot of combat decks using dominate.

Even if you don't agree that it's a good combat card, then this might
still be appropriate. One of the tenants of the game is that disciplines
don't get good cards in areas that they're not strong in because it would
upset play-balance. Thus, Celerity - a mostly combat discipline - doesn't
get very good stealth cards. If you need Celerity stealth, you get the
likes of Alacrity, which compared to Obfuscate stealth frankly sucks.
Likewise, if you need Dominate combat, you get Thoughts Betrayed. And
you're *lucky* to have it so good. A lot of people think Dominate gets
*WAY* too many of the cool cards in the game.

Fred

One is a 6-cap. Two are 8-caps. Four are 9 or 10-caps.

the measly 3 available to the Lasombra. And including the 'big'
vampires makes it 16 to 7; lots in favor of the warlocks.

Andrew, I realize that Rush decks are kicking you around like a little
lost puppy right now because you haven't learned to defend against
them yet. But combat is the WEAK THIRD of the 3 main strategies, and
rewriting Fame as you suggest would merely make combat weaker; every
deck that wanted to avoid combat would drop Fame on its key vampire.
Stupid on the face of it.

Not to mention what I can do to break this errata; I use the Tremere,
I make someone with AUS/tha (Richard Tauber!) famous. I intercept my
prey's actions, and play Burst of Sunlight at inferior. Now my prey,
who was the ACTING MINION, loses 3 pool, no matter if his minion
prevents the damage or not. If he plays S:CE, great! My guy doesn't
go to torpor either and is ready to intercept the next action.

>But what bugs me about the current errata to Fame is that it's an
>absurd gift to rush decks - the opposite of the original intent.

And combat decks damn well needed it, too. A simple Minion Tap/5th
deck, or a Consanguineous Boon deck, or ANY effective form of bloat
when combined with basic combat defense, will never be ousted by a
Rush deck. Sure, you eventually run them out of Fortitude, but those
MT/5th that they got off before you did that made it impossible to
bleed through before your predator killed you.

>That's the trouble with all the major errata that I've seen - they are
>hamfisted and distort the original intent too much.

That's because the original intent, on some cards, sucked ass and was
too easily broken. Original intent of the DESIGN is what we wish to
preserve; not original intent of any given card. I doubt the
designers wished the Gangrel to be able to send themselves to torpor
at will, bleeding their prey happily, unblockably, and unbounceably.

-- Derek

inherent limitations on Rush decks--I use one, and regularly use it to casue my
prey to lose 4 pool, but that is all. It usually doesn't net me much more than

Messages.Author: Frederick Scott
Messages.Body:
"Andrew S. Davidson" wrote:
> I don't play RPGs. I expect a good CCG to have a strong theme and to
> be consistent with it. This then affords opportunity for role-playing
> as well as strategy and tactics. These are several different
> dimensions to games:
>
> luck <------> skill
> theme <------> abstract
> simple <------> deep
> fuzzy <------> strict
> manual <------> mental
> social <------> competitive

Many of these are not really dimensions. The worst one is the "manual vs.
mental" thing because these are actually two possibilities out of many.
You are describing the challenge that a game poses, and other choices might
be involve speed (mentally or physically or both), awareness of surroundings
(remember the game "spoon"?), spatial relationships, intimidation and/or
bluffing, actually lots of things. Some are more mental, some are more
physical, some can be both or either.

Thinks like luck and skill or social and competitive can be more or less of
both.

Simple vs. deep can describe multiple separate aspects of a game: rule
structure vs. strategies. Most people enjoy their games with simpler
rule structures but deeper strategy choices. There is often SOME connection
between the two - thus making this a tricky order. But the connection is
far exact or necessary.

Theme vs. abstract is probably the only correctly "dimensional" thing you
nailed. I'm not ever sure what "fuzzy vs. strict" could mean but I have a
strong suspicion it turns out to be the same concept as one or more of the
others, when analyzed.

Fred

bears absolutely no relationship to an RPG, which is where
role-playing belongs.

Trying semantics is simply a waste of your and my time, as it's
awfully easy to spot the difference and call "bullshit".

>A Malkavian player acting his role as you describe might be equally
>vexing in the RPG or LARP - such is the nature of the Malkavians. In

In the RPG, however, it is appropriate; and in the RPG, a Storyteller
can make sure that the Malkavian acting in this fashion does not
destroy the game for everyone else.

In the CCG, a person taking random cross-table actions will quickly
upset the balance of the table and make it very little fun for
everyone involved. It is FAR more vexing to have someone being stupid
in the CCG.

>the CCG, I enjoy playing cards like Game of Malkav because they allow
>me to operate on both levels - that of the mad Malkavian and also the
>canny tactician. Players who only operate on one level are missing
>out.

Cards like Game of Malkav are part of the game, and while they have an
inherent flavour of "madness" about them, still have the potential to
work to your benefit. Calling a KRC and assigning 2 points of damage
to your grandprey and 2 to your grandpredator is not likely to EVER
work to your benefit, except in certain very narrow, obvious cases.

> Tom says that it was dominated by combat decks.

The idea is something like this: One combat deck can torporize
a fair number of vampires belonging to its predator and prey.
However, this generally sets up the two people not sitting next
to it to get easy VPs (or a free ride from their predator).

But if there are two combat decks on one table, then all of the
other three decks can be attacked by them, generally resulting
in greatly reduced efficacy of those decks. (If the two combat
decks are sitting next to each other, there is one player not
adjacent to a combat deck, but since Bum's Rush can be directed
at any player, they aren't actually safe from being Rushed, though
their vamps will probably be lower-priority targets than those
belonging to the Meths actually next to the combat decks.) So,
when there are at least two combat decks on a table, it's usually
possible for them to beat up the majority of the other vampires
on the table, allowing them to operate with relative impunity and
get at least a couple VPs each.

(This, too, is less good when they're sitting next to each other;
it may be possible for the predator combat deck to strike a deal
with the prey combat deck that the prey will be allowed to get
three VPs and then roll over and let the predator get the last two.
If that deal can't be arranged, though, the combat decks may end up
fighting each other more than is healthy for them and allow one of
the non-combat decks to oust them both.)

>

> a necessary part of this that they should be authentic - true to their
> background.

Hmmmm. Then it sounds like many of the people you're arguing with
here have a higher tolerance for abstraction in their CCGs than
you do. I like the theme of VTES, but it's the gameplay that I
find the most interesting thing about the game, and to my mind it
*is* a fairly abstract game. Not as much so as, say, bridge, but
about as much as, say, Magic.

I suppose. Still, if you pursue such a role with any kind a vigor,
to the point that it becomes more important than sound, obvious strategy
decisions, then you automatically mess up the game. However you may
feel about roleplaying games, a CCG - or at least *this* CCG (I'm not
saying it's not possible to create such a CCG) - is *not* one. It's a
zero sum board game, not designed to assume the players are doing anything
except maximizing their return on victory points.

Comes down to it, a player could play for any motivation that turns him
on. Roleplaying, frustrating another particular player, maximizing his
or her chances for sexual fulfillment, whatever. But since the game is
designed and balanced to assume what people want is only victory points,
things will get all of whack if someone starts taking on other motivations.
And other players are liable to resent you for that and cease playing with
you if you take it too far.

Fred

Messages.Author: James Coupe
Messages.Body:
In article
<06F0BEEE6CF70060.A8D9094B...@lp.airnews.net>,
Andrew S. Davidson <a...@csi.com> writes

>But why is the combination of two combat decks different from the
>combination of a combat deck and a vote deck, say? Is there a
>"comrade in arms" effect which causes the combat decks to work
>together?

It's the same with any two similar deck types. Since any given deck can
only ever have so much defence against <strategy>, if there are two
decks both carving it up with <strategy> they do better, since they both
manage to empty its hand much more quickly.

This becomes much more obvious with combat decks, since the end result
of a combat deck is more spectacular to watch, but it happens with many
deck types.

On any table where two combat decks do *not* sit together, they have at
least one common enemy when the game starts (their predator or prey).
They can both carve this deck up, as they would normally, but neither
has to waste as many cards on it as they would normally since there is
another combat deck doing some of the work. This then frees them up to
spend more of their time than usual attacking their respective preys and
predators, for offence and defence purposes.

Similarly, two vote decks will exhaust another deck's intercept, vote
defence, vote cancelling or whatever much more efficiently than just
one.

Such things remain relatively constant, whether they co-ordinate their
attacks or not.

I'll add that you've probably noticed that combat decks do really well in
2-player games or when there's only 2 players left. That's because they are
moving their prey closer to death at the same time they are keeping their
predator from ousting them. Having multiple combat decks at the table
mimics that effect.

I'd also say that 2-combat does better than 1 combat + 1 [other deck]
because pool loss attacks don't have as immediate an effect on how much
damage you'll be taking on your predator's next turn. If you are natural
allies with a vote deck and then your ally makes your Malk predator lose 8
pool from a couple of votes, there is little to keep him from sending a
govern + conditioning your way on his turn. Two rush combat decks can
better get the job done by removing the threat altogether.

Andrew wrote:
>>What are we supposed to make of the posters here who, with one breath,
say that rush decks don't win tournaments and, with the other, say
that that's what they play?>>

As a guy who pretty much exclusively plays Rush decks in competition, I can say
that:

A) Rush decks *can* win tournaments, they just don't do so often because not
many people play them (if more people were playing them, they would win more
often than they do, but not to an unacceptable level) and they are difficult to
win with, being obtuse in their path to victory and easily foiled.

B) Just because they don't win that often, it doesn't mean that it isn't worth
it to try.

>>And the general disdain for the player ratings?>>

There is a distain for player ratings because they don't really mean anything.

>>By their own account, it seems clear that many players are not in the
business of maximising their VPs.>>

No, that is not true at all. People who play Rush decks (well, smart people,
anyways) at tournaments are playing to win just as much as anyone else, and
are, in fact, attempting to maximize their VPs. It is just that the maximum
number of VPs attainable by a Rush deck is, generally, less than that of a
Bleed or Vote deck--the Rush deck isn't going to sweep all that often, and as
such, is going to get into the finals (if it does) by virtue of, like, 5 or 6
VPs, rather than 10.

>>This loose-cannon style makes me dislike the rush deck, exactly as you say.>>

And here you are making the faulty assumption that folks who are playing Rush
decks in tournaments are loose cannons. If they have any intention of winning,
they will not be doing this (as it is counter productive), just like any one
playing any other deck design. Yes, a Rush deck *can* be a random loose cannon,
but so can a vote deck ("Umm, I KRC the guy across the table for 3 pool,and
myself for 1..."), or for that matter *any* deck can be a loose cannon. If a
Rush deck is playing to win, it is not going to be a loose cannon, just like
any other deck.

Firm, etc.; I played Malk S&B once in my life (about a year after I

effective; I think I swept in 6-7 turns because everyone was wound up
on various forms of combat defense, and the one Rush deck at the table
was my grandprey and wasn't looking my way until it was too late. But
it wasn't especially fun; I didn't have to put much strategy or
thought into it at all. I prefer having to think and deal-make and
really CONSIDER my actions, as opposed to 'ok, should i bleed with the
Govern or the Scouting Mission this turn?'

Messages.Author: Frederick Scott
Messages.Body:


Your point is well-taken. I think your observation about rush decks
is valid and I'll say that I have the same misgivings about them for
exactly the reasoning that you're suggesting. It kinds of sucks to
find yourself the predator or prey of a rush combat as opposed to other
types of decks - which wouldn't bother me as much if they were effective
at winning the game.

I think what you're talking about is a desire to explore different
strategies in the game and to find a way to make them effective. You're
correct to point out such exploration represents a diversion from the
motive of absolutely maximizing victory points. In one sense, you can
consider it metagaming in that players are attempting to gain knowledge
of the workings of the game for purposes of long-term improvement in
their play at the expense of their effectiveness in the immediate game.
Because tournament play is considered to be more serious - the time when
short-term effectiveness is important - I guess that's one reason informal,
non-tournament play tends to get relegated to the function of experimenting
like that.

But clearly sometimes the bizarro deck is more about entertaining ourselves
than doing pure research. I guess folks tend to forgive that because
everyone pretty much understands the need to spice up the game with the
unusual. And I don't think role-playing the Malkavian or the other clans
is a bad thing to do for the same reasons. I'm just saying that none of this,
role-playing or pursuing bizarre card plays or combinations or whatever it
is, should be taken so far that the goal of ousting your predator gets
completely or nearly ignored. As long as people perceive that what you're
doing serves this end goal, you're probably OK. If they think you're just
doing basically random crap, they're going to get restive.

Fred

The winning chances have a lot to do with the number of players using
rush decks. A single one at a table has a great deal to do, much of it
to his predator. Once two rush decks appear, this changes. Provided
they can deal with one another, they should dominate most tables. Rush
combat seems to offer the greatest ability to intervene anywhere that's
required. This is a huge asset. One can imagine a critical mass being
reached in a playgroup or tournament scene where a substantial (more
than merely a dozen or so defensive cards) combat component becomes
essential for survival.

In a conversation I had with Skaff Elias, he said, "Oh, we had a bunch

format, at that time, bleeds were pretty silly, simply because other

the "interesting" choices out of WotC...

It was around before VTES.

People in Design "missed it" because, by and large, they were gamers
rather than true game theorists. I remember that when AI and the like
were printed, there was a huge <Boggle> response from the newsgroup,
mostly because people couldn't figure out why the cards were printed at
all.

> > AI being banned is silly, IMO. That should be reserved for broken
> > cards; and AI is undercosted, but not broken.

> Undercosted and *WRONG*! ;-)

Actually, calling it undercosted isn't quite right. More properly it
is overpowered.

Undercosted cards might have an acceptable effect, but for to cheap a
cost. E.g., "Jonny Underdog", Caitiff, 3, pot, pro, vic. Certainly
not overpowered, but definitely undercosted.

Overpowered cards have to strong an effect, even if they are close to
being the right cost. E.g., "Overwhelm", Animalism, 6 blood, Inf:
Return all animalism cards in your ashheap to your hand, discard down
to 7 cards. Sup: Put this card into play. Return all animalism cards in
your ashheap to your hand. You do not have to discard cards in excess
of seven in your hand. Do not replace non-animalism cards that are
played. Burn Overwhelm if your hand size is reduced to 6.

Clearly Overwhelm does too much, but it might actually have an
appropriate cost.

> I kinda like my fix, in that it is like a Sudden Reversal for
> bleeds (which is still inappropriate on the "methuselahs shouldn't
> intervene in little vampiric affairs that much" level, to my mind,
> but at least it doesn't burn anybody). But yeah, whatever.

hehe.

Mine is the opposite.

AI, Master-out-of-turn, 3 Pool, Burn a vampire bleeding you for more
than 3. That bleed IS considered successful.

AI is both undercosted and overpowered. I would considered it a
candidate for Broken, but really, that is a long debate...
